study_identification_part.si4_title: Lifespan development of thalamic nuclei and characterizing thalamic nuclei abnormalities in schizophrenia using normative modeling

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: To characterize age effects on thalamic nuclei volumes using normative models across the lifespan, clarify the association between cognition and thalamic nuclei volumes over time, and apply normative models to determine the frequency of thalamic structure abnormalities in individuals with schizophrenia and examine if deviation scores were associated with cognitive impairment.

rci9_site_effect_handling.detail: ComBat harmonization using neuroCombat R package; 12 sites total (9 from HCP Lifespan, 3 from Schizophrenia Cohort); preserved covariates: age, sex, race, diagnosis; empirical Bayesian framework for additive and multiplicative batch effects; harmonization performed prior to all analyses
rci9_site_effect_handling.supporting_text: To account for site effects, we used ComBat to adjust for site and scanner effects on both the HCP Lifespan Cohort and our Schizophrenia Cohort using the neuroCombat R package (https://github.com/Jfortin1/neuroCombat_Rpackage) prior to analysis. A key feature of ComBat is its ability to correct for the batch/site effects while preserving the inter-batch biological signals of interest by explicitly modeling and preserving the covariates of interest (including age, sex, race, and diagnosis). ComBat models the batch effects as additive and multiplicative components in the data and uses an empirical Bayesian framework to allow for robust estimation of batch effect parameters. Raw thalamic nuclei volumes extracted from THOMAS were harmonized for 12 sites (HCP Lifespan Cohort included 9 sites; Schizophrenia Cohort included 3 sites), with age, sex, race, and diagnoses included as covariates to adjust for during harmonization.

caa6_deviation_metric.answer: Centile scores; infra-normal (below 5th centile); normal (5th to 95th centile); supra-normal (above 95th centile); individual deviation maps coded as -1 (infra-normal), 0 (normal), or 1 (supra-normal)
caa6_deviation_metric.reason: The paper describes computing individual centile scores to place each individual based on their distance from the median of the age-normed, sex, and race-stratified distributions. Volumes were then categorized as infra-normal (below 5th centile), normal (5th-95th centile), or supra-normal (above 95th centile), creating individualized deviation maps.
caa6_deviation_metric.supporting_text: We computed individual centile scores for all individuals in our Schizophrenia Cohort to place each individual based on their distance from the median of the age-normed, sex, and race-stratified distributions provided by the reference sample (HCP Lifespan Cohort). This approach allows us to benchmark each individual's thalamic nuclei volumes by their typicality, with more atypical individuals having more extreme centile scores. Once centile scores have been calculated for each individual's set of thalamic nuclei volumes, we then categorized their volumes as either: 1) normal if their centile scores fell within the 5th and 95th centiles, 2) supranormal if their centile scores were above the 95th centile, and 3) infranormal if their centiles fell below the 5th centile. This classification provided individualized thalamus deviation maps in which each thalamus subdivision was numerically coded as 1 (supra-normal), 0 (normal), or -1 (infra-normal).

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Group differences in centile scores tested with Wilcoxon rank sum test for independent samples with FDR correction across 18 nuclei. Differences in proportions of individuals with infra-normal and supra-normal volumes between schizophrenia and healthy control groups tested with Pearson's Chi-squared test with FDR correction. Associations between deviation (centile) scores and cognitive function (SCIP composite z-score) tested using Spearman's Rho with FDR correction across 18 nuclei. Qualitative comparison of associations between centile scores versus standardized raw volumes (after regressing age, sex, race, ICV) with cognitive function.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: Up to 18% of individuals with schizophrenia exhibited abnormally small mediodorsal and pulvinar volumes (below 5th centile), and the degree of deviation, but not raw volumes, correlated with severity of cognitive impairment, demonstrating that normative modeling enables identification of individuals with thalamic abnormalities necessary for precision medicine.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: Normative models revealed diverse non-linear age effects across thalamic nuclei over the lifespan (ages 5-100+). Association nuclei (mediodorsal, centromedian, pulvinar) exhibited negative age effects during youth but stabilized in adulthood before turning negative again with older age. Sensorimotor nuclei (lateral geniculate, ventral posterolateral) remained relatively stable through youth and adulthood until declining with older age. Executive function showed a negative association with mediodorsal and pulvinar volumes in youth (development sample) but shifted to positive associations in young and older adults. In the schizophrenia cohort, significant group differences in median centile scores were found for bilateral pulvinar, mediodorsal, centromedian, medial geniculate, right lateral geniculate, and left anteroventral and ventrolateral nuclei. Individual-level analysis showed 14.1-17.9% of individuals with schizophrenia had infra-normal mediodorsal volumes and 15.0-17.5% had infra-normal pulvinar volumes, compared to 4.7-5.7% of healthy controls (chi-square p<0.001 for both). Bilateral medial geniculate also showed significantly increased proportions of infra-normal volumes. Importantly, centile scores but not standardized raw volumes showed significant associations with cognitive impairment (SCIP) in schizophrenia: bilateral mediodorsal (Right Rho=0.241, p=0.004; Left Rho=0.206, p=0.016) and pulvinar (Right Rho=0.185, p=0.022; Left Rho=0.198, p=0.016). The normative models generalized reasonably well to the independent schizophrenia cohort, with median 85.3% of healthy controls falling within the 90% normative range.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: Cross-sectional rather than longitudinal data; normative model starts at age 5 missing early development; multiple scanning parameters requiring data harmonization limiting ready applicability to new datasets; alternative factors co-segregating with schizophrenia (antipsychotic medication, adverse lifestyle factors) may contribute to deviant volumes
caa10_key_limitations.supporting_text: The dataset used to model typical development comes from cross-sectional, not longitudinal, studies ... Another limitation of our data was that we started modeling development at 5 years of age. While extensive development is expected after age 5, we are missing early development, especially in the nuclei where earlier development would be expected, such as the lateral geniculate nucleus ... the data used for both developing models of typical development and identifying deviation in schizophrenia were from multiple different projects with different scanning parameters, and data harmonization was necessary prior to analyses. As such, the models developed are not readily applicable to new datasets, and further work will be required to develop more flexible models ... Finally, alternative factors that co-segregate with schizophrenia, including antipsychotic medication and adverse lifestyle factors (e.g., increased substance use), may adversely impact the thalamus and partially account for the increased proportion of patients demonstrating deviant volumes

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: The study validated that normative models trained on multi-site HCP data generalized well to an independent single-site clinical cohort despite different scanners and acquisition protocols, with ComBat harmonization applied across all 12 sites. The use of centile-based deviation scores showed qualitatively stronger associations with cognition compared to raw volumes standardized for covariates, suggesting deviation scores may be more sensitive metrics for brain-behavior associations in clinical samples. The authors note that while group-level case-control differences are robust, only a minority of patients (up to 18%) demonstrate unusually small thalamic nuclei volumes, highlighting the importance of individual-level characterization for precision medicine.

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: The study examined 9 thalamic nuclei bilaterally (18 total regions): first-order nuclei (LGN, MGN, VPL, VA, VL) and higher-order nuclei (AV, PU, MD, CM). Cognitive assessment differed between cohorts: HCP used NIH toolbox executive function composite (average of Flanker, Dimensional Card Sort, Pattern Completion), while schizophrenia cohort used SCIP composite z-score. The study used age-unadjusted cognitive scores to examine age-by-cognition-by-volume associations across developmental stages. Data storage and processing at Vanderbilt University Institute of Imaging Science XNAT. Imaging pipelines containerized using Singularity and accessible via GitHub (https://github.com/baxpr/thomasdocker). Statistical analysis code at GitHub (https://github.com/Woodward-Lab/NormModThalamicNuclei). Three scanning sequences used in schizophrenia cohort, all Philips Intera Achieva 3T with different parameters (see Supplementary Table 3). HCP datasets acquired on Siemens Prisma 3T (HCP-D and HCP-A) and Siemens Skyra 3T (HCP S1200).
